title: SQL vs NoSQL
subtitle: Watch one online shop send each kind of data to the store whose shape fits its access pattern.
learn: How relational tables, schemas and joins let you ask questions you did not plan for
What key-value, document, wide-column and graph stores each optimize
Why NoSQL stores usually require you to design around known queries
How to choose a store by access pattern instead of by hype
Why most systems start with one relational database and add others only when forced

steps.title: One shop, five kinds of data
steps.body: An online shop stores orders, login sessions, a product catalog, a firehose of click events, and a 'people also bought' network. Each has a different shape and is read in a different way. Should they all live in one database, or does each deserve its own? The numbers in this lesson are rough single-node figures to show orders of magnitude, not benchmarks.
steps.idea: Pick a database by how the data is read and written, not by whether it is called SQL or NoSQL.
steps.caption: Five data shapes, five candidate stores.

steps.title: Orders in tables with a schema
steps.body: A relational database stores rows in tables with fixed, declared columns: customers, orders, order_items. The schema is a contract the database enforces, including types, foreign keys (a column that must point at a real row in another table) and uniqueness. Placing an order touches several tables, and a transaction makes them succeed or fail together. A well-tuned PostgreSQL node typically handles from a few thousand multi-statement write transactions to tens of thousands of simple queries per second, depending on hardware.
steps.idea: A relational schema trades flexibility for guarantees: the database itself rejects bad or half-written data.
steps.caption: A checkout transaction writes three tables atomically.

steps.title: Ask a question nobody planned for
steps.body: Next quarter someone asks: revenue per product category for customers who signed up in Berlin. Because data is stored once in normalized tables (each fact stored once), one SQL query can join customers, orders, items and products to answer it. No one had to predict this question when designing the tables. On a shop-sized dataset with indexes this report runs in a second or so; it is slow-ish but possible with no redesign (and heavy reports like this belong on a replica or warehouse, covered later). That ad hoc power is the main reason relational databases are the default.
steps.idea: Normalized tables plus joins let you answer new questions without changing how data is stored.
steps.caption: One query joins four tables on demand.

steps.title: Sessions: give me the value for this key
steps.body: A login session is read on every request and is only ever fetched by its session id. A key-value store such as Redis (or the simplest use of DynamoDB) maps a key to a value and is built around lookup by that key. Because there are no joins or ad hoc queries to plan, and Redis keeps data in memory, a lookup takes about half a millisecond and one node serves 100 thousand or more operations per second. Disk-based stores like DynamoDB are typically single-digit milliseconds. Sessions in an in-memory store need persistence or replication if they must survive a restart.
steps.idea: A key-value store is the fastest design when the only question is 'what is stored under this key?'
steps.caption: GET by session id returns in under 1 ms.

steps.title: Catalog: one product, one document
steps.body: A laptop has RAM and ports; a T-shirt has size and fabric. Forcing both into one table means many empty columns or many joined tables. A document store such as MongoDB keeps each product as one JSON-like document with whatever fields it needs, so a single read returns the whole product page. The cost is that by default the shape is enforced by your code rather than the database (some stores let you opt in to validation), and cross-document joins are limited and often slower at scale.
steps.idea: Documents fit data that is read and written as a self-contained unit with varying fields.
steps.caption: One read returns the full product document.

steps.title: Click events: huge write volume
steps.body: The shop logs 200 thousand click events per second during a sale, spread over a 5-node cluster (about 40 thousand writes per node). A wide-column store such as Cassandra or ScyllaDB spreads data by a partition key (say user id) and keeps rows inside a partition sorted by a clustering key such as time. Writes are cheap appends, and 'latest 50 events for user 42' reads one sorted slice. Design the table per query; other columns are not queried efficiently. Such stores usually favor availability and can return slightly stale reads by default (see Replication).
steps.idea: Wide-column stores scale writes by making every query hit one partition, so the table is designed around the query.
steps.caption: Writes fan out by partition key across the cluster.

steps.title: Recommendations: follow the relationships
steps.body: 'Customers who bought this also bought...' means walking from a product to buyers to their other purchases, two or three hops deep. In SQL each hop is another join, here a self-join (a table joined to itself, following product-buyer-product links). With indexes two or three hops are fine, but intermediate results multiply and deep or variable-length paths become awkward and slow. Many graph databases store each node's neighbours directly, so a traversal costs about the edges visited rather than the table sizes. Real recommendation systems often precompute results, so graphs earn their place when live path queries are the product.
steps.idea: Pick a graph store when queries are about paths and neighbours several hops deep.
steps.caption: A multi-hop traversal follows stored edges.

steps.title: Run the finance report on the document store
steps.body: Suppose orders had been put in the document store because it was fashionable. The revenue-by-category question now needs data from three collections. A document store can join across them (MongoDB has $lookup), but those joins are limited compared with a relational engine's and are not what the data model is optimized for. So you either combine orders, products and customers in application code, or copy product and customer fields into every order. Assume the app fetches a quarter of orders and joins in code; that takes seconds. Copies must be kept in sync.
steps.idea: NoSQL stores make known queries fast by pre-shaping data; unplanned queries then cost you code or copies.
steps.caption: Cross-collection joins are limited, so the app does the work.

steps.title: Start boring, add stores on evidence
steps.body: A common mistake is to adopt five databases on day one. As a rule of thumb, a single relational database, with good indexes and read replicas, handles most products well past a million users, and it gives transactions, constraints and joins for free. Add a key-value cache when reads hurt: the app checks it first, reads SQL only on a miss, then fills the cache. Add wide-column or time-series storage when writes outgrow one node, a graph store when traversals dominate. Each added store means more operations work, and cached copies can go stale, so you must decide when to expire or refresh them.
steps.idea: Every extra database is a new thing to run, back up and keep in sync, so add one only for a measured need.
steps.caption: SQL is the source of truth; others serve special reads.

steps.title: Choose by access pattern
steps.body: Relational suits structured data, joins and transactions, and answers questions you did not plan for. Key-value is fastest for lookups by key. Documents suit self-contained records with varying fields. Wide-column scales heavy writes when queries are known and partition-aligned. Graphs suit deep relationship queries. Ask how the data is read and written, how it must stay consistent, and how big it gets, then choose. The line is blurry: Postgres stores JSON documents in JSONB columns, and document stores such as MongoDB now offer multi-document transactions, so choose by access pattern and consistency needs, not by label.
steps.idea: List your queries first; the store that serves them directly is usually the right one.
steps.caption: Each store matches one access pattern.

quiz.q: Your team must answer a brand-new analytics question tomorrow that combines customers, orders and products, and nobody planned for it. Which design makes that easiest?
options: A key-value store keyed by order id
Normalized relational tables queried with joins
A wide-column table designed for the click-event query
Denormalized documents with product data copied into each order
quiz.why: Normalized tables store each fact once, so joins can combine them in ways nobody anticipated. The other designs were shaped around specific known queries.

quiz.q: A service only ever fetches a user's session blob by session id, millions of times per second. What is the best fit?
options: A graph database
A relational database with many joins
A document store with secondary indexes on every field
A key-value store
quiz.why: The only access pattern is lookup by key, which is exactly what key-value stores optimize, with no query planner or joins to pay for.

quiz.q: In a wide-column store you need to list a user's latest events, and later also list all events from one country. Why is the second query a problem?
options: The table is partitioned by user, so a country query would scan every partition unless you add a second table laid out by country
Wide-column stores cannot store country values at all, because columns must be declared up front for every row
Country lookups require a graph traversal, because a wide-column store cannot follow relationships otherwise
Wide-column stores only support writes, so every read has to go through a separate search engine
quiz.why: Data is placed by partition key and efficient queries must supply it. A different query needs a differently keyed copy of the data.

quiz.q: Which statement about 'NoSQL scales, SQL does not' is most accurate?
options: It is true for writes only, because SQL databases serialize all writes on one machine
It is false: NoSQL stores are slower than SQL on every workload, so they never scale better
It oversimplifies: NoSQL stores often scale out by limiting query types, while a single SQL node already handles very large workloads
It is true because NoSQL stores never need indexes and so avoid the overhead that limits SQL
quiz.why: Scale-out comes mostly from restricting queries to one partition, not from the data model's label. One relational node often serves many products, and databases that spread SQL across many nodes also exist.

quiz.q: You store each order as a document that embeds a copy of the product name and price. A product is renamed. What is the main consequence?
options: Old orders automatically update, because the store tracks references to the product
Order reads become slower, because each document must be rewritten on every read
The document store rejects the rename until every order embedding the old name is migrated
Existing orders keep the old copy, so you decide whether to leave or update them
quiz.why: Embedding duplicates data for fast single-read access. Sometimes keeping the price paid at purchase time is desired, but other copies need explicit synchronization.

cheatsheet.def: The declared structure of data. SQL enforces it on write; many NoSQL stores leave it to application code by default (schema-on-read, meaning the shape is interpreted when data is read), though some offer optional validation.
Storing each fact once across related tables to avoid duplication. Joins reassemble the data at query time.
Copying data into the place it is read to avoid joins. Reads get faster; writes must keep copies in sync.
Maps a key to a value and is optimized for lookup by key; no joins or ad hoc queries (some stores add data structures or sort keys). Examples: Redis, DynamoDB.

Stores self-contained JSON-like records with flexible fields. Good for read-as-a-unit data such as catalogs. Joins across collections exist (MongoDB $lookup) but are limited compared with a relational engine's joins. Example: MongoDB.
Partitions rows by a key and sorts them within the partition. Built for heavy writes and known queries. Examples: Cassandra, ScyllaDB.
Stores nodes and edges and traverses relationships directly. Best for multi-hop questions like recommendations or fraud rings.
Write down your top queries and consistency needs first. Default to relational; add a specialized store only for a measured mismatch.
